title: Apheresis Safety: Citrate, Replacement Fluids, ASFA Categories and Red Cell Exchange
summary: Recognize and treat citrate toxicity, anticipate the complications of plasma exchange and albumin replacement, read ASFA categories and grades correctly, and know the goals of red cell exchange in sickle cell disease.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 42 Hit 5 (citrate toxicity), Hit 11 (ASFA categories), Hit 12 (red cell exchange in SCD) and Trap 5 (citrate and magnesium). Checked against Warner 2025, Jerman 2026, Jacobs 2026, Reyes 2026, Jones 2026 and the ASFA tenth-edition abstract (Zantek 2026). The reviewer’s RCE target “HbS < 30%” is one indication-specific goal; Jones 2026 reports chronic-transfusion goals of 30–50% and wide variation between centers. Not taught: calcium gluconate dose and infusion time, circuit ionized-calcium targets, ACE-inhibitor withholding (Hit 6), the 10.5 mL/kg circuit limit (Hit 10) and Gilcher’s rule (Hit 3) — not in the sources read.

objectives: Explain how citrate anticoagulates and why it causes hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia and metabolic alkalosis.
Anticipate depletion coagulopathy and other complications of plasma exchange with albumin replacement.
Interpret ASFA categories I–IV and separate them from the strength and quality-of-evidence grade.
State the goals of red cell exchange in sickle cell disease and why it is preferred for chronic transfusion.

scenes.title: Dizzy at the apheresis chair
scenes.altText: A patient on an apheresis machine (centrifuge bowl token, tubing). Halfway through, the patient feels dizzy with chest discomfort, and the blood pressure dips. A nurse token holds a calcium syringe. Two more cards wait: “Is this procedure even indicated?” and “Sickle cell patient next: red cell exchange.” The cartoon scientist checks the anticoagulant bag labeled ACD-A (citrate).

cues.text: Halfway through a plasma exchange, the patient feels dizzy and has chest discomfort, and the blood pressure dips.
The anticoagulant in the machine is citrate. It keeps the blood from clotting in the tubing, but it also enters the patient.
Three questions today: what citrate does to the patient, how we know a procedure is worth doing, and what red cell exchange aims for in sickle cell disease.

scenes.title: How citrate anticoagulates — and what it steals
scenes.altText: A citrate token grabs calcium (Ca²⁺) tokens in the circuit: clotting needs calcium, so blood in the tubing stays fluid. When the blood returns, citrate also binds the patient’s calcium and magnesium (Mg²⁺). A symptom ladder: chest discomfort, dizziness, hypotension → severe hypocalcemia: seizures, QT prolongation. A treatment token: calcium (gluconate, chloride or carbonate) is given to prevent or treat it. A liver token: the liver metabolizes citrate to bicarbonate → metabolic alkalosis, which can worsen hypokalemia.

cues.text: Clotting needs calcium. Citrate binds calcium in the circuit, so blood in the tubing cannot clot.
When the blood returns, citrate keeps binding calcium, and magnesium too, inside the patient.
In one large series, low calcium most often showed up as chest discomfort, dizziness and low blood pressure. Severe drops can cause seizures and a prolonged QT interval.
So calcium, as gluconate, chloride or carbonate, is given to prevent or treat it. Magnesium can fall too, so it needs checking as well.
The liver turns citrate into bicarbonate, which can cause metabolic alkalosis, and alkalosis can drive potassium down.

scenes.title: What else falls during plasma exchange
scenes.altText: A results card from one center’s TPE series: most common complications — depletion coagulopathy (≈ 48%), hypocalcemia (≈ 44%), hypokalemia (≈ 37%). A replacement-fluid card: albumin replacement removes clotting factors without replacing them → low fibrinogen; plasma (FFP) is used when fibrinogen is low, bleeding risk is high, or in TTP. Other risks: infections after immunoglobulin depletion, hyperglycemia from the dextrose in ACD-A, transfusion reactions with plasma. A hypotension token: the most common intraprocedural event in another center’s series (≈ 2.6% of procedures).

cues.text: In one center’s plasma-exchange series, the most common problems were depletion coagulopathy in about half, low calcium in 44 percent and low potassium in 37 percent.
Why coagulopathy? With albumin as the replacement fluid, clotting factors are removed and not replaced, so fibrinogen falls.
Plasma is used as replacement when fibrinogen is low, bleeding risk is high, or the disease itself needs plasma, as in TTP.
Removing antibodies also lowers protective immunoglobulins, raising infection risk. The dextrose in the anticoagulant can raise glucose.
During the procedure itself, low blood pressure was the most common event in another center’s large series, in about 2.6 percent of procedures.

props.title: Replacement fluid
lines: Plasma: low fibrinogen, bleeding risk, TTP

scenes.title: Is it indicated? ASFA categories — and red cell exchange
scenes.altText: An ASFA card: indications are categorized I–IV and graded (GRADE-style strength 1 or 2, evidence A–C). Category I = first-line; II = second-line; III = optimal role not established; IV = ineffective or harmful. A caution token: in the guidelines, nearly a third of Category I indications rest on low-quality evidence, yet most carry strong recommendations; categories change between editions (e.g., ANCA vasculitis moved to Category III in 2023; the tenth edition was published in 2026). Then a red-cell-exchange card for sickle cell disease: chronic transfusion keeps HbS at a goal (often 30–50%); ASH recommends automated red cell exchange over other methods to limit iron loading; institutions vary in end-hematocrit and HbS targets.

cues.text: The American Society for Apheresis grades every indication. Category one is first-line therapy, category two second-line.
Category three means the best role is not yet established, and category four means apheresis is ineffective or harmful. Each also gets a strength grade, one or two, and an evidence grade.
Be careful: nearly a third of category one indications rest on low-quality evidence. And categories change between editions; ANCA vasculitis moved to category three in 2023.
Red cell exchange in sickle cell disease replaces the patient’s sickle cells with donor cells. Chronic programs keep hemoglobin S at a goal, often 30 to 50 percent.
Automated red cell exchange is preferred over simple transfusion to limit iron loading, though targets for hematocrit and hemoglobin S vary between centers.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards appear in turn: “Citrate only lowers calcium” (✓ it binds magnesium too — check Mg; metabolic alkalosis can follow); “Albumin is a complete replacement fluid” (✓ it does not replace clotting factors — watch fibrinogen; use plasma in TTP); “Category I means high-quality evidence” (✓ category reflects role; nearly a third of Category I rests on low-quality evidence).

cues.text: Trap one: citrate only lowers calcium. No. It binds magnesium too, and its breakdown can cause metabolic alkalosis.
Trap two: albumin replaces everything removed. No. Clotting factors are lost, so fibrinogen falls; plasma is needed in some cases.
Trap three: category one means strong evidence. No. The category is the role of apheresis; the evidence grade is separate, and often low.

props.title: ✗ “Category I = high-quality evidence.”
lines: ✓ Category = role; evidence grade is separate

scenes.title: Citrate steals two, leaves a base
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Citrate steals two and leaves a base.” It steals calcium and magnesium, and leaves bicarbonate behind (alkalosis). And: “Category is the job, grade is the proof.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: citrate steals two and leaves a base. It takes calcium and magnesium and leaves bicarbonate behind. And for ASFA: category is the job, grade is the proof.

Where it breaks: citrate effects depend on dose, infusion rate and liver function; replacement choices depend on the disease; categories change between editions; and red cell exchange targets differ by center and indication.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Citrate binds Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ → dizziness, chest discomfort to seizures/long QT · give calcium · alkalosis, low K⁺”, “Albumin: no clotting factors · ASFA I–IV = role, grade = evidence · RCE limits iron, HbS goal often 30–50%”.

cues.text: Citrate anticoagulation lowers calcium and magnesium and can cause alkalosis, albumin replacement depletes clotting factors, and ASFA categories describe the role of apheresis while a separate grade describes the evidence.

props.label: Citrate binds Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺ → dizziness … seizures/long QT · calcium · alkalosis, low K⁺
Albumin: no factors · ASFA I–IV = role, grade = evidence · RCE: less iron

explanation.what: Plain language: the anticoagulant in apheresis machines, citrate, grabs calcium and magnesium; plasma exchange removes good proteins along with bad ones; and guidelines rate how useful apheresis is for each disease. Scientific terms: ACD-A, ionized hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, depletion coagulopathy, replacement fluid (albumin, plasma), ASFA categories and GRADE, red cell exchange (RCE), HbS%.
explanation.why: Citrate chelates divalent cations (calcium, magnesium) needed for coagulation and neuromuscular function; the liver metabolizes it to bicarbonate. Albumin replacement restores oncotic pressure but not coagulation factors or immunoglobulins. RCE removes sickle cells while adding donor cells, limiting net iron gain.
explanation.measure: Watch ionized calcium, magnesium, potassium, fibrinogen. Common TPE complications in one series: depletion coagulopathy ≈ 48%, hypocalcemia ≈ 44%, hypokalemia ≈ 37%; hypotension ≈ 2.6% of procedures in another. Chronic transfusion HbS goals often 30–50%.
explanation.differs: ASFA category (role of apheresis) vs grade (strength of recommendation and quality of evidence); albumin vs plasma replacement; RCE vs simple transfusion.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: symptoms of low ionized calcium during apheresis → citrate → calcium; magnesium falls too; low fibrinogen after albumin TPE; ASFA category meanings; RCE preferred to limit iron.

questions.stem: During plasma exchange with ACD-A anticoagulant, a patient develops dizziness, chest discomfort and a falling blood pressure; ionized calcium is low. What is the most likely cause and response?

options.text: Citrate-induced low ionized calcium — give calcium and check magnesium
options.rationale: Correct. Citrate binds calcium (and magnesium); calcium is given to prevent or treat it.
Incorrect. TPE more often lowers potassium.

options.text: Allergic reaction to albumin — stop and give epinephrine
options.rationale: Incorrect. The low ionized calcium points to citrate effect.

options.text: Air embolism — place the patient head-down
options.rationale: Incorrect. The symptoms fit citrate toxicity.

questions.stem: After several plasma exchanges with 5% albumin replacement, a patient’s fibrinogen is low before a planned biopsy. What explains this?

options.text: Depletion coagulopathy: clotting factors were removed and albumin does not replace them
options.rationale: Correct. Plasma can be used as replacement when fibrinogen is low or bleeding risk is high.
Incorrect. Citrate binds calcium; it does not destroy fibrinogen.
Incorrect. Removal by exchange is the expected cause.
Incorrect. Albumin lacks clotting factors; it is not an anticoagulant.

questions.stem: An ASFA indication is listed as Category I with a 1C grade. What does this mean?

options.text: Apheresis is first-line therapy, with a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence
options.rationale: Correct. Category describes role; 1 = strong recommendation; C = low-quality evidence.
Incorrect. Grade C indicates low-quality evidence.

options.text: The role of apheresis is not established

claims.text: Citrate binds calcium and magnesium; hypocalcemia symptoms (chest discomfort, dizziness, hypotension; severe: seizures, long QT); calcium given; metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia.
TPE complications: depletion coagulopathy, hypocalcemia, hypokalemia; albumin lacks factors; plasma for low fibrinogen/bleeding/TTP; infection, hyperglycemia; hypotension 2.6%.
ASFA categories I–IV and GRADE; low-quality evidence common in Category I; ANCA vasculitis to III in 2023; tenth edition 2026.
Chronic transfusion HbS goal often 30–50%; ASH prefers RCE to limit iron; targets vary.
Perioral/acral paresthesia as the early sign; calcium gluconate 10 mL over 10–15 min; circuit ionized calcium 0.2–0.3 mmol/L; RCE end Hct ~30%.
